brief_context: Describes the climate which affects meal planning for weekends.
brief_extract:
Fruit Delight (British Farm Produce Council)

A LITTLE MORE TIME
If time permits it is helpful to plan ahead for weekend meals. With the English climate it is best if dishes are two-fold in that the dishes can be eaten at home or quickly packed for a picnic. Provided food is adequately packed and if possible chilled in the refrigerator till the last minute, sandwiches, meat and sweet dishes will travel well.

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of student ratios in higher education.
article_title: Speech by the Secretary of State for Education and Science
brief_extract: In 1969 for every 10 boys with three or more A level passes entering university, there were 5 girls; for every 10 boys with two A levels going to university only 4 girls. Among undergraduates in British universities in 1969 for every 10 men there were only 4 women. On full-time and sandwich advanced courses in further education, including those at polytechnics, in 1969 the ratio of men to women was 10 to 3.

brief_context: Number of milk-producing farms in the UK.
brief_extract: The milk that is a daily occurrence on your very doorstep—about 16m doorsteps to be more precise—has a whole series of laws to ensure its purity. There are approximately 115,000 milk-producing farms in the UK and most of the milk is collected in churns or bulk tankers. brief_context: Location of the Church of England Primary School.
brief_extract:
Junior workshop with small electric cooker and electric pottery kiln. New concept for village school

EASTERGATE Church of England Primary School near Chichester, Sussex, is an exciting and unique new school and contrasts in every possible way with its 138-year-old predecessor. It is all-electric and the first school building in this country to be planned and constructed by an 'integrated design' process, which requires the closest possible co-operation from the beginning between the headmistress, the architect, the design and building teams in order to ensure that the design for the building's shape, fabric and internal environment are integrated from the initial stages.

Location of the Ergonomics Unit studying equipment heights for women.
brief_extract:
Heights of women
Some interesting frames deal with the heights of sinks, work tops and cupboards in relation to the heights of women. Some new thinking on this subject has been taking place in the Ergonomics Unit recently established at Loughborough University with the object of trying to get away from standard heights for equipment related to average heights for women and introducing more flexibility. When one realises that the heights of most women in this country vary between 4' 10" and 5' 10" (1,450 mm and 1,750 mm) with the 5' 4" (1,600 mm) group predominating, it is obvious that no one height of working surface or sink will be suitable for all women, nor will the same height be suitable for any one woman for all her kitchen tasks.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding electrical supply safety standards.
brief_extract:
Checking equipment
Besides photographs, many other souvenirs are brought home, especially from abroad; sometimes people bring back electrical appliances or lighting fittings and if you have done so it is most important to have the article checked by an Approved Contractor before it is put into use. The contractor will, of course, be entitled to charge for his time in checking the equipment, especially as it was not bought from him in the first place, but a check is essential because equipment which is accepted and used in other countries is not necessarily safe when used on the public supply in the UK. Apart from differences of supply voltage, there are differences in practice regarding the earthing of consumers' installations and different standards of construction.

location_standardised: Drury Lane, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Site of the original dairy started in 1896.
brief_extract:
The well stocked shelves, the display of goods,
some in refrigerated units specially designed
for Sainsbury's, and the presentation of tinned,
wrapped, packeted, frozen and fresh foods all
neatly labelled and priced and set out in a cool,
clean atmosphere are merely the tip of the
company's iceberg. Family tradition
The tradition of selling good food has its
origin in the family history of the firm from the
small dairy in Drury Lane, London, started
in 1896 by John James Sainsbury and his wife
Mary Anne, to the 212 stores now under the
chairmanship of John Sainsbury of the fourth
generation, who succeeded his uncle, Sir Robert
Sainsbury, in 1969. The two young pioneers
emphasised freshness and cleanliness at a time
when these conditions were not prevalent, and
it was their modest ambition to have a branch
for each of their six sons.

brief_extract:
John James had definite ideas
about shop layout, and in about 1876 had the
opportunity to really test his theories on pleasing

branch in Croydon using basically the same
interior shop layout of counters, with a work
area behind for the assistants and shelves on the
walls, room for a rank of customers and still
space for a woman to push her pram! To this,
however, he added ornate and elaborate
decoration, pillars, stained glass and wrought
ironwork.

brief_extract:
This vigilance is supplemented by an equally strict observance of hygiene at all the depots, factories and retail outlets within the framework of the company. 'Own label' products
In the Drury Lane dairy sausages and pies were sold under the sign 'my own make' and from this Sainsbury's continued to sell a few commodities, which they bought in bulk and sold under brand names until the outbreak of the Second World War. Few of the brand names survived the War, and branded goods enjoyed little success until Sainsbury's 'own label' instant coffee was launched with dramatically successful results.

brief_context: Where Clarence Birdseye discovered meat stays good when frozen.
brief_extract:
How it all started
The method of quick freezing that established
the modern frozen foods industry was invented
by an American with the unlikely name of
Clarence Birdseye. During a hunting trip in the
Arctic, he discovered that meat was still perfectly
good to eat several months after freezing and
that the quicker the temperature is lowered, the
better the quality of the food when it is finally
eaten. In 1917, he began experiments in the
kitchen of his home, freezing fish and rabbit
meat in small cartons.

brief_context: Region where the quick freezing industry began in 1945.
brief_extract:
He conceived the idea of
compressing the cartons between refrigerated
metal plates to achieve a rapid lowering of
temperature, a method still used for some
products today. The quick freezing industry in Britain got
going soon after the end of the war in 1945. Birds Eye Foods Ltd, a subsidiary of Unilever,
set up a factory in existing buildings on the
river bank at Great Yarmouth in Norfolk.

brief_context: Regional reference regarding soil warming operation durations.
brief_extract: The safest method is to use low voltage equipment but unfortunately this costs more. Normally if the unit is switched on 10 hours a night in the South and 12 hours in the North it is ample, adding an hour or two during really cold weather. However, to avoid the fag of switching on in the evening and off in the morning, which could involve a cold or wet trip to the bottom of the garden, operation of the warming unit can be controlled by time switch or capillary thermostat.

VISIT TO THE CENTRAL ELECTRICITY GENERATING BOARD SALMON HATCHERIES
by MRS. NAN BOND, B.A., Chairman, Bristol Afternoon Branch

The annihilation of salmon on the grids at the point of intake of river water for the cooling process at Generating Stations along the Severn Estuary created bad feeling among ardent fishermen. To placate them, and to keep the rivers stocked and make good the loss caused by their own undertaking, the Generating Board set up their Salmon Hatcheries at Llanfrynach.

brief_context: Location of the Salmon Hatcheries set up by the Board.
article_title: VISIT TO THE CENTRAL ELECTRICITY GENERATING BOARD SALMON HATCHERIES
brief_extract:
NAN BOND, B.A., Chairman, Bristol Afternoon Branch

The annihilation of salmon on the grids at the point of intake of river water for the cooling process at Generating Stations along the Severn Estuary created bad feeling among ardent fishermen. To placate them, and to keep the rivers stocked and make good the loss caused by their own undertaking, the Generating Board set up their Salmon Hatcheries at Llanfrynach. This station is manned by only two keen employees who work many hours during the winter in cold water and unheated sheds, cold water being essential to the rearing of the fish.

brief_context: Location of the EAW headquarters and food freezer exhibition.
brief_extract: A whole new lore on food freezing has been built up in recent years and the subject could become as much of a popular cult as flower arranging. To add to the store of knowledge and to provide information and impartial advice, the EAW has arranged at its headquarters in London a compre-hensive display of domestic food freezers, including chest and cabinet types and refrigerator/freezers, ranging from 1.75 cu ft to 10 cu ft in size. All the models on view have the approval of BEAB (British Electrotechnical Approvals Board for Household Equipment) or have been submitted for approval.

location_standardised: Foubert's Place, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The specific street address for the EAW exhibition in London.
brief_extract: With a freezer an inventory of contents is invaluable so that you know exactly what you have in stock and the date when each item was put in. The exhibition at headquarters is open to the public from 9.30 am to 5 pm Mondays to Fridays until early 1972 and it is hoped that many EAW members will take the opportunity to call at Foubert's Place to see it when coming to London for Christmas shopping* or after Christmas for the sales. The subject is of course a particularly topical one for EAW branches as most programmes will be including talks, demon-strations or discussions on food freezing as part of the current Food and Cookery theme.

brief_context: Where turkey farmers went to study farming methods.
brief_extract:
Thousands of pounds have been spent in
genetic research to change the old narrow-
breasted bird of pre-war days to the broad-
breasted turkey of today and there has been an
enormous increase in the ratio of meat to bone. Just after the war, half a dozen turkey farmers
went to America to study methods there. When
they came back they established turkey farming
on a new basis.

An extra special wine treat for the Christmas season could be a Beaujolais Vin de l'Année, which many traditional wine merchants are planning to have in their shops from early December. article_title: VISIT TO BONHOMIE HOME FOR THE DISABLED and VISIT TO HAMPSHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE, SPARSHOLT, NEAR WINCHESTER
brief_extract: Some of those who come here live for the most part of the year in one room and they cannot speak too highly of the care and attention they receive while staying at this delightful holiday home. This college, which with buildings and recreational areas now covers 437 acres, was first opened about 1868 on a site near Basingstoke but moved to Sparsholt in 1913. It is residential and has 77 students, both girls and boys.
